parts.title: Lena and the Last Pear
paras: Long ago, a hungry squirrel named Lena searched the forest for food. Winter was near, and the trees were bare. At last, she found one juicy pear under an old log.
Lena was about to eat it when she heard a tiny cry. A little mouse sat shivering in the cold. "I have not eaten in two days," the mouse whispered.

Lena looked at the pear. Then she looked at the mouse. She sighed, broke the pear in half, and gave the bigger piece to her new friend. Soon the mouse stopped shivering. The next day, the mouse showed Lena a hidden nest full of acorns. And that is why the forest folk say, "A kind heart is never empty."

parts.title: The Boastful Beetle
paras: Bo the beetle loved to brag. "I am the strongest bug in the whole meadow!" he told everyone. "I can lift a leaf over my head!"

One bright morning, a gust of wind blew a heavy twig onto the path. All the ants stopped. They could not get by. "Easy!" said Bo. He pushed and pushed. He puffed and grunted. But the twig did not move, and soon Bo was stuck beneath it, with his legs kicking in the air.

The ants worked together. They tugged the twig a little, then a little more, until Bo wiggled free. Bo blushed. "You are strong because you help each other," he said quietly. "Next time I will ask for help." From that day on, Bo bragged less and listened more.

parts.title: Why Geese Fly South Together
paras: Long ago, when the world was new, geese did not fly south for the winter. Each goose did whatever it pleased. The most stubborn goose of all was a young gander named Toma. "I go where I want, when I want," he liked to say.

One fall, the leaves turned gold and the wind blew cold. Old Grandmother Goose gathered the flock beside the lake. "Snow is coming," she said. "Soon the lake will freeze, and the grass will be gone. We must fly south, where the water stays open and the plants still grow. We will fly together, so no one gets lost."

Toma flapped his wings and laughed. "Not me. This lake is my home, and I will not leave it." The flock begged him to come, but Toma would not change his mind. So the flock flew off without him, honking good-bye in a long line across the blue sky.

For a few days, Toma had the whole lake to himself. Then the snow came. It fell for three days and three nights. The lake turned to ice, so Toma had no place to swim. The grass was buried under the snow, so he had nothing to eat. Toma grew thin and weak. At night he shivered alone on the frozen shore.

One gray morning, a crow landed beside him. "Your flock went south," said the crow. "Follow the river. It will lead you to them." Toma was tired, but he flew and flew along the river. Each day he flew a little slower. At last he heard honking. His flock was resting on a warm, open lake. Grandmother Goose spread her wings around him. "We knew you would come," she said.

Toma never forgot that hard winter. The next fall, he was the first goose to line up. And that is why, to this day, geese fly south together in a long V across the sky, calling to one another so that no one is left behind.

texts.label: Fact text

parts.title: On the Move: How Geese Migrate
paras: Every fall, you may hear loud honking high above you. Look up, and you might see a flock of Canada geese flying in the shape of a V. The geese are migrating. To migrate means to travel from one place to another when the seasons change.

Geese eat grass, seeds, and water plants. In winter, snow covers the ground and ponds freeze in many northern places. When food is hard to find, many geese fly south, where the weather is warmer and the water stays open. In spring, when the snow melts, they fly back north to raise their babies, called goslings.

Migrating geese often fly in a V shape. Scientists think the V helps the birds save energy. Each goose flies a little behind and to the side of the goose in front of it, where moving air helps lift its wings. Flying at the front is the hardest job, so the geese take turns leading. Their honking helps the flock stay together.

How do geese know where to go? Young geese learn the route by flying with their parents. Scientists believe geese also use the sun, the stars, and landmarks such as rivers, coastlines, and mountains to find their way.

Not all Canada geese migrate. In many towns and cities, including parts of Virginia, some geese stay all year long. Parks, ponds, and golf courses give them grass to eat and water that does not freeze. Because they can find food in winter, they do not need to make the long trip.

texts.label: Story
texts.title: Marla Barnes and the Mighty Storm

parts.title: Marla Barnes and the Mighty Storm
paras: Up in the hills of Virginia, on a farm with a red barn, lived the strongest girl who ever wore boots. Her name was Marla Barnes. On the day she was born, she let out a yell so loud that it shook the apples off every tree in the orchard. Her first word was "MORE!" and she said it to her mother's corn bread.

By the time she was five, Marla could carry a cow under each arm. By the time she was eight, she could plow the whole cornfield before breakfast, using a fork from the kitchen. Folks came from miles around just to watch her work, and they always left shaking their heads.

One hot summer, a storm started to grow far out past the mountains. It was the biggest, fiercest storm anyone had ever seen. Its clouds were as dark as a barn at midnight, and its thunder roared so loud that the stars hid. The storm was heading straight for Marla's town.

The people of the town met in the town hall to decide what to do. Some wanted to hide in their cellars. Some wanted to pack their carts and run. Everybody talked at once, and nobody could agree. Finally, Marla stood up. "Let's vote," she said. "Each person gets one vote, and the idea with the most votes wins." The people wrote their choices on scraps of paper and dropped them into a hat. When the votes were counted, most people had chosen Marla's idea: she would stop the storm herself.

Marla marched to the top of the tallest hill. The storm roared toward her, spinning faster than a top. Marla did not run. She reached up, grabbed the storm by its tail, and tied it in a knot. Then she swung onto its back and rode it like a wild horse.

The storm bucked and twisted for three days and three nights. It tore so hard at the ground that it scooped out a valley, and the valley filled with rain and became a lake. At last the storm grew tired. Marla steered it to the seashore and set it gently down over the ocean, where it turned into a soft, warm rain.

When Marla came home, the whole town cheered. They voted again, and this time every single vote said the same thing: Marla Barnes was the town's hero. If you visit those hills today, you can still swim in the lake that the storm dug, the summer Marla Barnes rode it out to sea.

texts.label: Fact text
texts.title: Every Vote Counts: How Voting Works

parts.title: Every Vote Counts: How Voting Works
paras: Imagine your class has to choose a name for its new fish. Some students want Bubbles. Others want Captain Fin. How can the class decide in a fair way? One fair way is to vote. When people vote, each person gets one choice, and the choice with the most votes wins.

In the United States, adults choose many of their leaders by voting. Citizens who are 18 years old or older can vote for leaders such as the president, the governor of their state, and the mayor of their town. People also vote on questions, such as whether their town should build a new park. Election Day is the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.

On Election Day, many voters go to a polling place, such as a school or a library. Each voter gets a ballot. A ballot is a paper or a screen that lists the choices. The voter marks one choice for each question. In many states, including Virginia, people can also vote early or mail in their ballot.

Voting is private. Each voter marks the ballot alone, behind a screen or curtain, and no one else sees the choices. Because the vote is secret, people can choose what they really think without worrying that someone will be upset with them.

After the polls close, workers count the ballots carefully. The choice with the most votes wins. When a choice gets more than half of all the votes, we say it has a majority. Sometimes an election is very close, and just a few votes make the difference. That is why people say every vote counts.

parts.title: Shirley Burke Digs a River
paras: In the dry hill country there once lived a girl named Shirley Burke. She was so quick that she could turn off the light and be in bed before the room got dark. Her curly hair was so thick that birds built nests in it, and she never minded one bit. She could whistle louder than a train, and she once outran a jackrabbit just to say good morning.

One summer, no rain fell for forty days. The sun burned the grass brown, and the dirt cracked into a thousand pieces. The town well went dry. The cows in Farmer Hurd's herd were so thirsty that they mooed in a whisper, and even the frogs packed their bags and hopped away.

The town council met to solve the problem. The council members talked about digging a new well, but the ground was as hard as rock. They talked about carrying water from the Silver River, but the river was a three-day walk away. No one could think of a plan that would work.

Then Shirley spoke up at the meeting. "If the town can't go to the river," she said, "I'll bring the river to the town." The council members laughed, but Shirley did not. She rolled up the sleeves of her shirt, picked up a shovel, and started to dig.

Shirley dug so fast that dirt flew up like a fountain. Rocks, roots, and old stumps leaped out of her way. In the first hour she dug a mile. By sunset she had dug all the way to the Silver River. When she lifted her last shovelful, the river burst through with a roar and came rushing down her ditch, curving and turning all the way to town.

The people cheered and splashed. Farmer Hurd's cows drank until their bellies were as round as barrels. The council voted to name the new river after Shirley, and they made a new rule: no one may ever waste a single drop of its water.

That is why, if you visit the dry hill country today, you will find a river with more twists and turns than a curly ribbon. People say it curves because Shirley stopped to say hello to every family on her way to town. Some folks say that on hot summer evenings, you can still hear Shirley humming as the water rushes by.

texts.label: Fact text
texts.title: Who Makes the Rules in Your Town?

parts.title: Who Makes the Rules in Your Town?
paras: Every community has rules. Some rules tell drivers how fast they may go. Others say when the library is open or where dogs must wear a leash. Rules made by a government are called laws. Who makes the laws for a town?

In many towns, a group of people called the town council makes local laws. The people of the town vote to choose the council members. The council meets in public, often once or twice a month, to talk about problems and decide what to do.

Many towns also have a mayor. The mayor leads the town and works with the council. In some places the mayor runs the council meetings and helps plan how the town will spend its money. The mayor also speaks for the town at special events, such as the opening of a new library.

First, someone notices a problem, such as cars driving too fast near a school. Next, the council talks about the problem at a meeting and listens to what citizens think. Then the council members vote on a new rule, such as a lower speed limit. If the rule passes, the town puts up signs so everyone knows about it.

Council meetings are open to the public. Citizens can come to a meeting, share their ideas, and ask questions. Even kids can write a letter to the council. When citizens speak up, leaders learn what the community needs.
parts.caption: Neighbors share ideas at a town council meeting. Anyone can come and listen.

texts.label: Story
texts.title: Joy Howard and the Voice That Saved the Town

parts.title: Joy Howard and the Voice That Saved the Town
paras: In a little town by the sea lived a girl named Joy Howard, and Joy had the loudest voice in the world. When she was a baby, her cry could knock the crows out of the trees. When she sang in the shower, the fish in the bay popped their heads out of the water to listen. Her laugh was so big that it once blew the hat off the mailman two streets away.

Joy's voice made some people grumble. "Joy, please don't shout," her mother would say. "Use your inside voice." Joy tried. She whispered, she murmured, and she mumbled. But even Joy's whisper could rattle the windows on Main Street, and her mumble could be heard in the next town.

One autumn night, a thick fog rolled in from the ocean. It was so thick you could cut it with a spoon. Out at sea, the fishing boats were heading home, but the fishermen could not see the shore. They called out to one another, but they could barely see the ends of their own boats. To make matters worse, the town's foghorn had broken that very morning. Without the horn, the boats might crash into the rocks.

The mayor ran through the town looking for help. "Somebody has to call the boats home!" she cried. People shouted from the docks, but the fog swallowed their voices. Then the mayor remembered Joy Howard.

Joy climbed to the top of the lighthouse. She took a deep breath, all the way down to her toes, and she shouted, "THIS WAY HOME!" Her voice boomed across the water like a giant drum. It bounced off the clouds and rolled over the waves. Out in the fog, the fishermen heard it. They turned their boats toward the sound and followed it, one by one, safely into the harbor.

The next day, the whole town gathered in front of the town hall. The mayor gave Joy a shiny brass crown that said Official Town Voice. Joy wore it every day. From then on, nobody asked Joy to use her inside voice, and whenever the fog rolled in, she climbed the lighthouse stairs two at a time. And on foggy nights, sailors say you can still hear her calling across the bay.

texts.label: Fact text
texts.title: Lights and Horns: How Lighthouses Keep Sailors Safe

parts.title: Lights and Horns: How Lighthouses Keep Sailors Safe
paras: For hundreds of years, sailors have faced a big danger near the shore: rocks hidden under the water. At night or in a storm, a ship could crash before the crew ever saw land. Lighthouses were built to warn sailors and guide them safely home.

A lighthouse is a tall tower with a bright light at the top. Lighthouses stand on rocky points, on islands, and at the edges of harbors. Because the tower is so tall, sailors can see its light from many miles away. Many lighthouses are also painted with bright stripes or patterns so sailors can spot them in the daytime.

Each lighthouse flashes its light in its own pattern. One might flash every five seconds. Another might flash twice and then go dark. By counting the flashes, sailors can tell which lighthouse they are looking at and figure out where they are.

Thick fog can hide even the brightest light. So many lighthouses also had a fog signal, such as a bell or a foghorn. The loud, low sound traveled through the fog and warned sailors that land was near.

Long ago, lighthouse keepers lived at the lighthouse. Every night they climbed the stairs to light the lamp, and they polished the glass so the light would shine brightly. Today most lights turn on by themselves, and ships also use computers and satellites to find their way. One of the oldest lighthouses in the country, the Old Cape Henry Lighthouse, was finished in 1792 and still stands in Virginia Beach.
